title: When a reply fails — what the chat should offer

steps.path: The red box that replaces a reply when the provider fails
steps.headline: Should a failed reply get a Try again button that re-runs it, without you retyping your message?
steps.today: When a provider fails after the app's own retries, the reply is replaced by a red box with the provider's words. To carry on you type a new message, often "continue". Only a reply that stalled mid-way has a Try again button today.
steps.problem: Typing "continue" adds a new message to the conversation each time, and it is not obvious that this is the way forward. Your Opus conversation needed it three times in a row.
steps.proposal: Try again would re-run the reply that failed, using the message you already sent. Nothing new appears in the conversation, and anything the assistant already did in that turn stays done.

options.label: When trying again can help
options.summary: Shown for a busy or unreachable provider and for errors the app does not recognise; hidden for a bad key, no credit or a used-up plan.
pros: Never offers a button that can only fail again.
An error the app does not recognise still has a way forward.
cons: An account problem has no Try again — you fix it first, then press send.

options.label: On every failed reply
pros: One button you can always find in the same place.
cons: Pressing it after a bad key or no credit only shows the same error again.

options.label: No — keep typing a message
cons: Every failure still costs a new message to recover from.

steps.path: The red box, when the reason is your account
steps.headline: When the problem is your account — a rejected key, no credit left, a spending cap — what should the box offer?
steps.today: A rejected OpenRouter key or an expired ChatGPT sign-in shows Open settings; too little OpenRouter credit shows Add credit. A rejected Anthropic or OpenAI key, Anthropic's monthly spending cap, and OpenAI's used-up quota show only the provider's words, with no button.
steps.problem: For those last cases you have to work out yourself where the fix is — a settings screen in the app, or the provider's own website.
steps.proposal: The app now tells these apart, so each could get the button that fixes it.

options.label: The button that fixes it
options.summary: Bad key → Open settings (to the right provider). No credit, spending cap or used-up quota → a button to that provider's billing page. Plus Switch model, so you can carry on with another one now.
pros: One press to the place that actually fixes it.
Switch model lets you keep working while the account is sorted out.
cons: Up to two buttons in the box instead of one.

options.label: Open settings only
cons: For billing problems settings cannot fix it — you still go to the provider's website yourself.

steps.path: The red box, when the conversation is too long for the model
steps.headline: When the conversation has grown too long for the model, should the box offer to summarise it and carry on?
steps.today: When a conversation outgrows the model, the app already summarises older messages on its own and tries once more. If that still fails, you see the provider's words — "prompt is too long" — and nothing to press.
steps.problem: The fix exists (the summary button in the context panel), but nothing points you to it, so the conversation looks broken.
steps.proposal: The box would say the conversation is too long for this model and offer Summarise and continue: older messages become a short summary, and the reply is tried again. Switch model would sit beside it, for a model with a bigger window.

options.label: Summarise and continue + Switch model
pros: Switch model keeps every message for a model that fits them.
cons: Summarising loses detail from older messages (the summary stays visible in the chat).

options.label: Summarise and continue only
cons: No way to keep every message, short of opening the model picker yourself.

steps.headline: Should the box say what happened in plain words, with the provider's own message folded underneath?
steps.today: The box shows the provider's message as it came, for example "Overloaded (provider error 529)" or "You have reached your monthly spend cap". Some are clear, many are not.
steps.problem: "Provider error 529" means nothing to most people, and the wording changes from provider to provider for the same problem.
steps.proposal: One plain sentence per kind of problem, naming the provider — e.g. "Anthropic is overloaded right now.", "Anthropic stopped this reply: your monthly spending cap has been reached." — with the provider's exact words under a Details fold. An error the app does not recognise keeps showing the provider's words in full, never a guess.

options.label: Plain sentence, details folded
pros: You can tell at a glance whether to wait, fix your account, or shorten the conversation.
The exact provider message is one click away for a bug report.
cons: One extra click to see the provider's exact words.

options.label: Keep the provider's words
cons: Stays as unclear as it is today.

steps.path: The "thinking" line while the app waits to try again
steps.headline: While the app waits to try again after a busy or unreachable provider, should the thinking line say so?
steps.today: The app now waits and tries again for up to about a minute when a provider is busy or unreachable. During the wait the thinking line shows the existing "taking a while… trying again in 8s" countdown, the same one used when a reply goes quiet.
steps.problem: That line does not say why it is waiting, so a busy provider and a slow model look the same.
steps.proposal: The line would name the reason — "Anthropic is busy — trying again in 8s", "Can't reach Anthropic — trying again in 8s" — with Stop available as today.

options.label: Name the reason
pros: You know whether to wait or switch models.
cons: A few more words on the line for a short time.

options.label: Keep today's countdown
cons: A busy provider still looks like a slow model.

steps.path: The end of a reply that ran out of steps
steps.headline: When a reply stops because it used up its allowed number of steps, should it offer Keep going?
steps.today: Long tasks can stop with the line "Response ended: max_steps." — a code word — and no button. This happened 38 times in your conversations, mostly with ChatGPT and DeepSeek.
steps.problem: The wording is not plain, and the only way on is to type a message.
steps.proposal: The line would read "Stopped after 150 steps." with a Keep going button that continues the same task for another round of steps. (Changing the step limit stays in Settings.)

options.label: Plain line + Keep going
pros: One press to carry on, no message to type.
cons: Easy to keep pressing on a task that is going in circles.

options.label: Plain line only
pros: Makes you look at the work before it carries on.
cons: Still costs a typed message to continue.
